input.text: You've arrived at the Ming Tombs — the valley where thirteen emperors of the Ming dynasty sleep beneath the mountains. The site was chosen by feng shui masters: mountains arc around it like dragon wings, and a river winds through — an emperor's paradise. Every visitor walks the Sacred Way first: a several-kilometer avenue lined with colossal stone statues — two rows of creatures, from camels and elephants to mythical qilin and xiezhi, each carved from single blocks five centuries ago. They stand guard in pairs: one kneeling, one standing — so that even a tired spirit guard never sleeps on duty. At the end, the archway and the dragon-phoenix gates frame your approach to the tomb valleys. Only one tomb has ever been opened: Dingling, the Underground Palace, excavated in the nineteen fifties — step down into the vaulted chamber of stone and stand where the Wanli Emperor was laid to rest with his two empresses. The mountains hold the rest — thirteen emperors, one valley, five hundred years of silence.
